Given a hypothesis function $h(x)$, the loss function $l: (h(X\_n), Y\_n) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ takes the hypothesis function's prediction (i.e. In the case of binary classification, a common loss function that is used is the $0$-$1$ loss function:. In general, the loss function that we care about cannot be optimized efficiently. For example, the $0$-$1$ loss function is discontinuous. So, we consider another loss function that will make our life easier, which we call the **surrogate loss function**. An example of a surrogate loss function could be $\psi(h(x)) = \max(1 - h(x), 0)$ (the so-called hinge loss in SVM), which is convex and easy to optimize using conventional methods. This function acts as a proxy for the actual loss we wanted to minimize in the first place. Obviously, it has its disadvantages, but in some cases a surrogate loss function actually results in being able to learn more. results.title: Conducting a Power Analysis to Determine Sample Size
results.content: # Conducting a Power Analysis to Determine Sample Size. ## What is Statistical Power? Statistical power is defined as the probability that a study will correctly reject the null hypothesis when it is in fact false. Common thresholds for power are 80% or 90%. Therefore, when power is 80%, there is a 20% chance of a Type II error occurring. Ensuring this threshold statistical power is reached ensures the study is capable of detecting true effects. ## Key Components of Power Analysis. There are five key components to power analysis that interact to ensure the study has enough participants. * **Power Level:** Power is the complement of the probability of a Type II error, or failing to reject a false null hypothesis. The most common power level is 80%, which means there is a 20% chance of a Type II error occurring. * **Sample Size:** The number of participants in the study directly impacts power. Larger sample sizes have lower variability and therefore higher power as there is a greater chance of detecting a true effect. If data is more spread out, larger sample sizes will be required to reach adequate power. ## Steps to Conduct a Power Analysis. A lower significance level and higher power level will require larger sample sizes. ## Common Tools for Power Analysis. Power analysis to determine adequate sample size is a very broad field with a lot of specialty applications and knowledge. In these cases, it is advisable to conduct a pilot study and gather preliminary data to get an estimate of what the effect size may be. This is especially important in longitudinal studies, but it is important to enroll more participants than your power analysis calculations say you need. This way, if participants leave the study, do not fully complete the data collection process, or otherwise have unusable data, power can still be met with the remaining participants. Depending on the complexity of your study, power analysis may become very complicated. Power analysis is an essential part of designing a statistically rigorous study. By considering effect size, significance level, power, sample size, and data variability, researchers can calculate the number of participants needed to achieve reliable results.
